more_beautiful.reason: A is richer and more finished. The luggage-tag hero, the confident slab-serif hierarchy, the warm paper palette and the well-built cards and form chips hold together better than B's flatter, sparser layout, which leaves dead space and mixes mint, grey, yellow and magenta.

less_generic.reason: B carries one idea all the way through: a ticket-stub wordmark standing in for the missing logo, the date highlighted inside the headline, tear-off arrival-time tickets and a ticket at the end. Apart from its luggage tag, A follows the familiar AI landing-page pattern (eyebrow, two-tone slogan, icon cards, numbered three steps, three-column dark footer) in the common cream-and-terracotta style.

better_overall.reason: A gives the cafe a more complete and welcoming page. It has a one-step booking flow with a choice of dates, an email-or-phone confirmation, a copy and phone fallback, a setup prompt for the organiser and a Find us section. That outweighs its placeholder contact details and made-up house rules, which the owner can edit, while B leaves out the venue and contact details and makes people go through two booking steps.

A: Luggage-tag hero shows the next date at a glance with a live 'Tomorrow' countdown, the hours, last arrivals and the venue; the favicon matches the tag
Detailed can-fix cards with icons, a can't-fix list with reasons, and a 'Not sure? Email a photo' option for anything in between

Booking lets visitors choose from the next three Saturdays, pick from compact 3x2 time chips and icon item chips, and give email or phone. Submitting opens a pre-filled email in one step, with a copy-text and phone fallback, an optional form-service endpoint and a honeypot
Careful accessibility: skip link, fieldsets and legends, inline errors that move focus to the first problem, visible focus rings, reduced-motion and print styles
Works without JavaScript (falls back to 'first Saturday of every month' and a mailto form), and a visible organiser note flags the example email until it is replaced
Friendly British copy that suits a volunteer group: bring it clean, chargers, access needs, volunteering call
B: The next date sits inside the headline itself, highlighted, with the hours, so it can't be missed on any screen
A ticket idea specific to this cafe: the wordmark stands in for the missing logo, the arrival slots look like tear-off tickets showing the window ('to 10:30'), and submitting produces a ticket
Honest and lean: no invented address, phone or house rules; the example booking address is labelled as such to visitors; the can't-fix list keeps to defensible safety exclusions
Very accessible form: error summary with jump links, inline errors, 'Error:' prefix in the page title, visible native radios, large touch targets, live status messages
Distinctive system-font pairing (DIN-style display with Charter body) and high-contrast colour blocks; short page that reaches the booking form quickly on a phone

A: Shows a placeholder venue ('Church Street, Your Town AB1 2CD') and a real-looking phone number (01632 960123) without flagging either on the page; 'Open in Maps' searches for the placeholder address
Makes up house rules and claims the owner never gave: one item per booking, people with a slot seen first, 'later slots are usually quieter', no volunteers for phones or laptops
Apart from the tag, the structure and the cream-and-terracotta styling feel like a stock AI-generated template
Long page on mobile (about 7,600px): the hero button falls below the first screen and the form is far down
Until the owner sets the email, a loud dashed organiser note sits at the top of the booking form where visitors can see it
B: Booking takes two steps ('Get your ticket', then 'Email your ticket'), which adds friction and may make people think they have booked when they have not
Only the next session can be booked; there is no venue address, map, contact email or phone, or explanation of how the morning runs, and the footer is minimal
Desktop layout feels sparse and unfinished in places: empty space to the right of the hero, an empty left column beside the form, and a bare lower half in the can't-fix band
The palette feels pieced together, and six fully saturated yellow tickets stacked on mobile are visually loud even before one is selected
The owner gets no clear prompt to replace the example booking address, and the date written into the HTML goes out of date if JavaScript fails
